query: Eutectic high-entropy alloys contain dual-phase lamellar colonies with numerous internal boundaries, where microcracking can initiate and lead to catastrophic damage during room-temperature tensile deformation. Conventional processing commonly raises strength at the expense of ductility, while the wide range of previously proposed microstructural-design and processing strategies has not eliminated room-temperature brittleness and limited tensile ductility. Under these constraints, what single intervention could improve both strength and room-temperature tensile ductility? State one testable hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts outcomes relative to the unmodified lamellar-colony baseline, defines its boundary conditions, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: A minor alloying addition of Boron, introduced during casting followed by a controlled homogenization and annealing process near the eutectic temperature, will lead to exclusive segregation of Boron at the internal lamellar interfaces of eutectic high‐entropy alloys (e.g., AlxCoCrFeNi). This targeted boundary modification will enhance interfacial cohesion and pin boundaries, thereby improving both yield strength and room-temperature tensile ductility compared to an unmodified lamellar-colony baseline.
generation.material_initial_state: Eutectic high-entropy alloy with dual-phase lamellar colonies produced via conventional casting, exhibiting internal boundaries that are prone to microcrack initiation during tensile deformation.
generation.intervention: Introduce a minor amount of Boron during alloy fabrication, followed by a controlled homogenization and annealing treatment at temperatures near the eutectic point to promote exclusively boundary-segregated Boron, while avoiding the formation of brittle secondary boride phases.
generation.conditions: The alloy is processed by conventional casting and then subjected to a heat treatment near the eutectic temperature that is precisely optimized to achieve uniform Boron segregation at the internal lamellar interfaces without precipitating brittle borides.
generation.structural_mediator: Boron-enriched internal lamellar interfaces with improved cohesion.
generation.mechanism: Boron atoms preferentially segregate to the inter-lamellar boundaries during the annealing process, thereby enhancing interfacial bonding. This increased cohesion not only impedes microcrack initiation during tensile loading but also provides effective pinning of the boundaries, which contributes to precipitation-like strengthening without compromising ductility.
generation.predicted_outcome: The treated alloy is expected to display a higher yield strength due to enhanced boundary pinning, and improved room-temperature tensile ductility as a result of reduced microcrack nucleation at the reinforced interfaces, in comparison to the untreated, conventional lamellar-colony alloy.
generation.baseline: The performance of the unmodified alloy, processed via conventional casting and heat treatment without Boron addition.
generation.boundary: The intervention is effective only if the Boron segregates exclusively to the internal interfaces; if excessive or non-uniform segregation occurs leading to the formation of brittle boride phases, the desired improvements in strength and ductility may not be realized.
generation.uncertainty: The precise magnitude of the improvement in strength and ductility remains to be quantified and will depend on the narrow processing window that ensures selective Boron segregation. There is uncertainty regarding the optimal Boron content and heat-treatment parameters that avoid detrimental phase formation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of alloy samples: one with the minor Boron addition and optimized heat treatment, and a control set without Boron. Utilize atom probe tomography (APT) or high-resolution transmission electron microscopy (HRTEM) to assess Boron segregation at the boundaries. Perform room-temperature tensile tests to measure yield strength and ductility.
measurements: Quantitative analysis of Boron concentration and its distribution (e.g., exclusively at the lamellar interfaces)
Microstructural analysis to detect any formation of secondary brittle boride phases
Tensile yield strength and ductility (percent elongation to failure)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If Boron is found to form non-uniform segregation or precipitate as brittle borides, or if the mechanical tests do not show statistically significant improvements (or show deterioration) in yield strength and tensile ductility compared to the control alloy, then the hypothesis will be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Realizing improved strength–ductility synergy in eutectic alloys acting as in situ composite materials remains a challenge in conventional eutectic systems, which is why eutectic high-entropy alloys (EHEAs), a newly-emerging multi-principal-element eutectic category, may offer wider in situ composite possibilities. Here, we use an AlCoCrFeNi2.1 EHEA to engineer an ultrafine-grained duplex microstructure that deliberately inherits its composite lamellar nature by tailored thermo-mechanical processing to achieve property combinations which are not accessible to previously-reported reinforcement methodologies. The as-prepared samples exhibit hierarchically-structural heterogeneity due to phase decomposition, and the improved mechanical response during deformation is attributed to both a two-hierarchical constraint effect and a self-generated microcrack-arresting mechanism. This work provides a pathway for strengthening eutectic alloys and widens the design toolbox for high-performance materials based upon EHEAs. Boron has also been widely added in alloys to improve the cohesive strength of grain boundaries [], e.g., to change the fracture mode of Ni3Al from intergranular to transgranular and thus prevent early failure [], or to lower the migration rate of grain boundaries and inhibit grain growth at high temperatures []. Additionally, the short-range order in an Fe40Mn40Co10Cr10 alloy caused by the addition of boron atoms or the precipitation of borides was reported to retard the motion and increase the density of dislocations [], and the discontinuous intergranular precipitation of borides in high-strength steels avoided the intergranular fracture [], both improving the mechanical properties of the alloys [,]. As the grain-boundary brittleness is a major issue for BCC RHEAs, a minor amount of boron element (0.1 at.%) was hence added into an HfMoNbTaTiZr RHEA in the present study for potential precipitation of borides at the grain boundaries and improvement of grain boundary cohesion, then to yield a larger work hardenability and better ductility.

proposals.material_system: Eutectic high‐entropy alloy (e.g. AlxCoCrFeNi) with dual-phase lamellar colonies
proposals.intervention: Minor alloying addition of a boundary‐segregating element such as Boron
proposals.conditions: Prepare the alloy via conventional casting followed by a controlled homogenization and annealing process near the eutectic temperature to encourage Boron segregation exclusively at the internal lamellar interfaces
proposals.mechanism: Boron atoms preferentially segregate to the inter-lamellar boundaries, enhancing interfacial cohesion and bonding. This improved cohesion both impedes microcrack nucleation under tensile stress and provides grain-boundary pinning that contributes to strengthening without sacrificing ductility
proposals.predicted_outcome: The Boron-doped alloy is expected to show simultaneously higher yield strength (via enhanced boundary pinning) and improved tensile ductility (via reduction of crack nucleation from interfacial weaknesses) relative to the undoped lamellar baseline
proposals.why_it_addresses_the_question: This single intervention directly tailors the internal interface chemistry—the most vulnerable sites for crack initiation—thus offering a unified route to overcome the trade-off between strength and ductility in eutectic high-entropy alloys

proposals.material_system: Eutectic high‐entropy alloy (e.g. AlxCoCrFeNi) with established dual-phase lamellar colonies
proposals.intervention: Tailored low-temperature annealing to induce in situ nanoprecipitation at lamellar boundaries
proposals.conditions: Post-solidification annealing at a sub-eutectic temperature (e.g. 20–50°C below the eutectic temperature) for a controlled duration to nucleate fine precipitates along the lamellar interfaces while avoiding overall microstructural coarsening
proposals.structural_mediator: Uniformly distributed nano-precipitates decorating the colony boundaries
proposals.mechanism: The mild annealing promotes the formation of nano-sized precipitates along the lamellar interfaces that act as crack arresters and enhance local bonding. Concurrently, the precipitate dispersion causes precipitation hardening, which elevates strength without reducing ductility
proposals.predicted_outcome: Compared to the untreated alloy, the annealed alloy is predicted to exhibit increased strength (due to precipitation hardening) and enhanced ductility (via improved load transfer and crack blunting at the boundaries)
proposals.why_it_addresses_the_question: This approach offers a single thermal treatment step that modifies the microstructure at the very sites responsible for brittleness, aiming to break the conventional strength–ductility trade-off in a controllable manner

proposals.material_system: Eutectic high‐entropy alloy (e.g. AlxCoCrFeNi) initially processed to yield coarse lamellar colonies
proposals.intervention: Rapid solidification via melt spinning to refine lamellar spacing
proposals.conditions: Melt spinning under high cooling rate (exceeding 10^5 K/s) to achieve a refined dual-phase microstructure, followed by minimal post-processing to retain the as-solidified features
proposals.structural_mediator: Refined, ultrafine lamellar colonies with reduced interlamellar spacing and more homogeneous internal boundaries
proposals.mechanism: The extreme cooling rate reduces the growth time of lamellar colonies, thereby refining the phase spacing and homogenizing the internal boundary structure. This reduction in scale minimizes stress concentration sites and microcrack initiation points while also promoting a fine-scale strengthening mechanism
proposals.predicted_outcome: The melt-spun alloy should demonstrate an improvement in both tensile strength (via microstructural refinement) and ductility (by reducing the severity and connectivity of internal stress concentrators) over the conventionally processed baseline
proposals.why_it_addresses_the_question: By acting exclusively through the solidification path, this single intervention improves the intrinsic microstructural architecture—transforming the colony boundaries from crack initiation sites to a more benign, uniformly distributed internal network—thereby concurrently enhancing strength and ductility

proposals.material_system: Bulk eutectic high‐entropy alloy (e.g. AlxCoCrFeNi) exhibiting dual-phase lamellar colonies
proposals.intervention: Application of laser shock peening (LSP) to induce beneficial compressive residual stresses at colony boundaries
proposals.conditions: Perform LSP at room temperature with optimized laser energy density and overlap to induce a deep compressive stress field specifically concentrated at the internal lamellar interfaces, while carefully controlling processing to avoid surface ablation
proposals.structural_mediator: Residual compressive stress state localized at inter-lamellar boundaries
proposals.mechanism: Laser shock peening produces high-magnitude compressive stresses that counteract the tensile stresses during deformation, thereby delaying or preventing the initiation and propagation of microcracks at the internal boundaries. In addition, the induced work hardening contributes to increased overall strength
proposals.predicted_outcome: Relative to the untreated baseline, the LSP-treated alloy is expected to yield higher tensile strength (from work hardening and residual stress stabilization) alongside enhanced ductility (via suppression of crack initiation at the boundaries)
proposals.why_it_addresses_the_question: This mechanical surface treatment targets the problematic internal boundaries in a single processing step, harnessing compressive residual stresses to robustly oppose the onset of brittle fracture while simultaneously strengthening the material

critiques.addresses_problem: Yes, it directly targets the vulnerable internal lamellar boundaries, which are the primary sites for microcrack nucleation in eutectic high-entropy alloys.
critiques.constraints: It respects the dual-phase lamellar colony system and uses conventional casting with an annealing step near the eutectic temperature. However, there is a risk that the minor alloying addition may inadvertently form unwanted secondary phases if not tightly controlled.
critiques.physical_soundness: The mechanism of boron segregating to grain boundaries to improve cohesion is physically sound and has precedent in related alloy systems.
critiques.feasibility: The processing steps (casting, homogenization, annealing) are well-established, making this approach feasible.
critiques.evidence: Prior studies have shown that boron additions can improve interfacial cohesion and alter fracture modes (e.g., evidence from PMC6353877 and PMC9572892).
critiques.main_risk: The risk lies in the possibility of forming brittle boride phases or non-uniform segregation that could compromise ductility.
critiques.fix: Introduce a precise control experiment to optimize boron content and heat-treatment parameters to ensure exclusive boundary segregation without promoting brittle phase precipitation.

critiques.addresses_problem: Yes, it aims to improve both strength and ductility by reinforcing the lamellar interfaces via nanoprecipitation, directly addressing the microcrack initiation issues.
critiques.constraints: It meets the constraints by modifying only the lamellar boundary regions without altering the overall dual-phase architecture, provided the annealing is carefully controlled.
critiques.physical_soundness: The mechanism is physically sound; fine precipitates can serve as crack arresters and contribute to precipitation hardening.
critiques.feasibility: Low-temperature annealing to induce nanoprecipitation is a standard method in alloy processing, though precise control over precipitate size and distribution is critical.
critiques.evidence: Recent studies (PMC6478865 and PMC7673736) support the notion that nanoprecipitation enhances strength while aiding ductility in related HEA systems.
critiques.main_risk: The primary risk is the difficulty in controlling the precipitation process; inhomogeneity or over-precipitation could lead to embrittlement or coarsening that adversely affect ductility.
critiques.fix: Refine and calibrate the annealing temperature and time to ensure a uniform, nanoscale precipitate formation exclusively at the lamellar interfaces.

critiques.addresses_problem: Partially. It aims to improve strength and ductility by refining the microstructure, but the intervention targets the colony size rather than directly reinforcing the weak internal boundaries.
critiques.constraints: While it respects the material system, rapid solidification via melt spinning is typically used for producing thin ribbons rather than bulk materials, potentially conflicting with application-scale constraints.
critiques.physical_soundness: The mechanism is generally sound as microstructural refinement often leads to enhanced strength and ductility; however, the scale and morphology changes may not be ideal for the dual-phase lamellar structure inherent to the alloy.
critiques.feasibility: Melt spinning is established, but transferring ultra-rapid solidification methods to produce bulk parts without losing the refined microstructure is challenging.
critiques.evidence: While evidence in PMC7075928 describes effects of refinement in lamellar structures, the use of melt spinning to achieve such refinement in bulk eutectic high-entropy alloys is not well supported.
critiques.main_risk: The main risk is that the processing may yield anisotropic, ribbon‐like microstructures that do not translate to bulk material performance and may introduce new defects.
critiques.fix: Couple the rapid solidification with subsequent consolidation techniques (e.g., stacking or additive manufacturing) to produce bulk materials that retain the refined lamellar architecture.

critiques.addresses_problem: Yes, it targets the problematic lamellar colony boundaries by introducing compressive residual stresses that can counteract crack initiation.
critiques.constraints: The approach conforms to the system constraints, but most laser shock peening (LSP) applications are limited to surface or near-surface treatments, which might not fully address internal lamellar interfaces in bulk samples.
critiques.physical_soundness: The underlying mechanism of using compressive residual stresses to inhibit crack initiation and propagation is well established; however, transferring these stresses uniformly to internal boundaries is more uncertain.
critiques.feasibility: Laser shock peening is an established process for improving surface properties, yet ensuring deep penetration of compressive stresses across the entire microstructure of a bulk alloy remains challenging.
critiques.evidence: Literature (e.g., PMC6353877 introduction, PMC7021732, and PMC7220923) supports LSP for improving strength–ductility combinations, but mostly in contexts where treatment depth is sufficient.
critiques.main_risk: The risk is that LSP may only modify surface layers and not impart the necessary compressive stresses at internal lamellar boundaries, limiting its effectiveness in preventing microcrack nucleation in bulk material.
critiques.fix: Develop a multi-pass or alternative LSP strategy to ensure that compressive residual stresses penetrate deeply into the bulk, particularly targeting internal lamellar boundaries.

decision.rationale: Direction A directly targets the vulnerable internal lamellar boundaries by using a minor Boron alloying addition, which is supported by prior evidence (PMC6353877 and PMC9572892) for enhancing interfacial cohesion and altering fracture modes. Although there is a risk of forming brittle boride phases, this risk is considered manageable by precisely optimizing the Boron content and heat-treatment conditions. Compared to the other directions, this approach most directly addresses microcrack initiation at the interfaces while offering a single‐step chemical modification intervention that can be readily implemented in conventional processing routes.
